Nature: According to the Dreamseeker Priest, a Wayob is "will without form or thought". Wayob are not physically present in Natlan, but can manifest there through obsidian totems and Nightsouls. They can see the past and future.

Each tribe has its own Wayob, and the dreams of the tribe's chief carry its will. People do not know why manifestations appear; the belief is that a Wayob sends one to solve a problem.

Society: The Wayob are central to tribal life. They choose certain members of a tribe to inherit Ancient Names. Because of the Abyss's long-lasting effects, Natlanese people without a Wayob's protection can suffer memory loss, stress and bad luck, so the tribes depend on them.

Relations: The Wayob serve their tribes; the Lord of the Night, as ruler of the Night Kingdom, is the god of the realm they inhabit. Known Wayob include Chaac, Angakuk, the Great Spirit of This Land (Children of Echoes), Maghan's master (Masters of the Night-Wind) and a Weakened Wayob Manifestation that appeared in the Biting-Cold form and, on the surface at Tecoloapan Bay, as an adult Iktomisaurus (5.2).

History: When the Abyss invaded the Night Kingdom, the Wayob became infected with Abyssal energy. This greatly weakened their bond with their tribes and put all of Natlan in danger (Past and Future). After the Night Kingdom was purged of its Abyssal influence, the Wayob went back to their normal duties. Shortly after that, they told Citlali that Xbalanque, the first Pyro Archon, was returning to the human world (After the Peace).

Status as of 7.1: As of 7.1 the Wayob are active again and protect their tribes as before. The wiki page records nothing later than the events above.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay guidance (project recommendation): Wayob speak through dreams, totems and tribal chiefs, not as ordinary persons. Do not give them faces, names or personalities beyond what canon says of individual Wayob. Natlanese characters treat them as ancestral wills and protectors.

348.content: Wayob Manifestations are obsidian totems that the Wayob use to appear in Natlan. In the game they are elite enemies in six elemental kinds (Flow-Inverted, Foliar-Swift, Rock-Cavernous, Biting-Cold, Burning-Aflame, Thundering). The people of Natlan do not know why they appear.

349.comment: Wayob: Myths of the Night Realm
349.content: This artifact text from the Obsidian Codex set tells how Chaac took fire from the Sage of the Stolen Flame, shared it with his tribe and defeated a wicked dragon. When he was old and alone, he lit the first flame on a mountain and called to his companions, and the god of the night realm answered. The text calls this the birth-cry of the first Wayob.

350.content:
Wayob Manifestation (also: Wayob Manifestations, Flow-Inverted Wayob Manifestation, Foliar-Swift Wayob Manifestation, Rock-Cavernous Wayob Manifestation, Biting-Cold Wayob Manifestation, Burning-Aflame Wayob Manifestation, Thundering Wayob Manifestation): Wayob Manifestations are elite enemies in Natlan, the form in which the Wayob revered by the six tribes show themselves on the land. They look like obsidian totems or statues and appear through totems and Nightsouls. There are six types, one for each tribe and element: Flow-Inverted (Hydro), Foliar-Swift (Dendro), Rock-Cavernous (Geo), Biting-Cold (Cryo), Burning-Aflame (Pyro) and Thundering (Electro).

The Adventurer Handbook says the Wayob worshipped by Natlan's tribes manifest themselves in these obsidian totems. Natlanese do not know why they appear; the belief is that a Manifestation is sent to solve some problem.

Nature: Archive text says the Wayob is a belief that grew from the tribes and obsidian totems once Natlan began to communicate with the realm of the Lord of the Night. A Wayob is a consciousness of collective thought and the home of the ancestors' souls.

Wayob have no fixed form and attach themselves to things in order to guide lost tribespeople. Storytellers often cast Manifestations as messengers of trials or guides to the Night Kingdom; a Saurian-Crowned Warrior is said to have fought one in a trance and learnt from it. Each type is a tribe's own Wayob, which the tribe believes controls a related power.

Society: Each tribe worships its own Wayob. According to their Archive entries: the People of the Springs believe theirs controls tides and waves, flowing and still water; the Scions of the Canopy, growth of fruit and leaf and the veins of leaves; the Children of Echoes, mountains, valleys and echoes of stone; the Masters of the Night-Wind, freezing and crystallisation, fixedness and mutability; the Flower-Feather Clan, fire, heat and blazing winds; the Collective of Plenty, thunder and speed, and abundant harvests.

Abilities and limits: Gameplay (not literal lore): a Manifestation periodically raises a ward and a field around itself. The ward blocks all damage, and the field drains Energy from the whole party while the active character stands in it.

If the ward is not destroyed before charging finishes, it turns into an elemental shield that must be removed with the right reactions. Destroying the ward earlier yields more elemental particles. Either way, breaking a ward stuns the Manifestation briefly. Each type uses its own element.

Relations: Manifestations are bound to the Wayob and the tribes, not to the Abyss. Hostile behaviour toward the Traveler is not explained by the Archive texts.

Individuals: The wiki lists a Weakened Wayob Manifestation among known Wayob individuals; the six types here are otherwise unnamed group forms.

Scene use: This project's suggestion (not canon): a Manifestation suits a scene of tribal ritual, trial or guidance at a totem, treated with the respect the tribes show it.

351.content: Natlan's six tribes each venerate a Wayob, a great spirit said to embody the will of the tribe's ancestors. Per the wiki, they are non-corporeal and dwell in the Night Kingdom; a tribe's chief hears their will in dreams. Manifestations are the form in which they appear in the world. See the creature entry for the Wayob themselves.

352.content:
Whopperflower (also: Whopperflowers, Cryo Whopperflower, Pyro Whopperflower, Electro Whopperflower, Vanagni, mimetic plant monster): Whopperflowers are elemental plant monsters found all over Teyvat. They hide as Sweet Flowers, Mint or Small Lamp Grass and burst out when someone tries to pick them, then fight with Cryo, Pyro or Electro. They have high resistance to every damage type, and given enough time and food they grow into huge Regisvines.

Cryo and Pyro Whopperflowers are present from Version 1.0; the Electro one was added in 2.0. The Adventurer Handbook calls them "a bizarre mimetic plant monster". The Aranara call them Vanagni.

Nature: Mimetic plants that lurk beneath the surface and ambush unsuspecting prey, taking years, plentiful nutrition and the right environment to put down roots and become a giant tree that sways and spews elemental power.

Archive text for the Pyro one says Teyvat hosts plants infused with the elements and that, having gained a measure of intellect, their "nutritional needs" have also greatly increased. The Electro one's text says that, fully charged, it can unleash a strong current from its crown, and that some researchers have tried to apply them in other fields.

Abilities and limits: They attack with their element, burrow underground to reposition, and periodically raise an elemental shield while charging up a special attack. Breaking the shield in time paralyses them and lowers their resistance.

Game mechanics (not narrative lore): the disguise can be told apart because a disguised plant does not sparkle, has no Elemental Sight silhouette, shows a dialogue bubble instead of a pickup icon, and does not glow at night when posing as Small Lamp Grass. Seed Dispensary and Nahida's All Schemes to Know do not pick them up. Unusually large clusters of one plant are often a clue.

Relations: Canon gives them no allies or masters; they are simply a hazard to travellers and farmers. The Aranara have their own name for them, Vanagni, from the quest The World of Aranara.

Individuals: Notable cases: during an Archon Quest a group posed as Glaze Lilies; in Sumeru commissions a single Whopperflower disguised as a budding Sumeru Rose freeloaded off the farmers' watering, then fled rather than attacked when revealed.

Scene use: Use Whopperflowers as a harmless-looking roadside trap: a too-perfect patch of flowers that does not sparkle. Keep them animal-like, without speech or malice.

353.content: Whopperflowers that feed long and uninterrupted become Regisvines: immobile, with a shield at the roots or corolla that greatly raises resistance. Breaking the shield with the right elemental reactions paralyses the Regisvine.

354.content: During the limited-time Dragonspine event Shadows Amidst Snowstorms, a mutated plant called the Fellflower took the form of Albedo. The wiki notes that mutated Whopperflowers can occasionally pose as humans; this is a special event case and not a habit of ordinary Whopperflowers.

355.content:
The Wild Hunt (also: Wild Hunt, Wasteland Wild Hunt, Wilderness Ghoul, Wilderness Ghouls, Wilderness Hunter, Wilderness Exile): The Wild Hunt is an Abyssal phenomenon, and the horde of monsters it produces, in Nod-Krai. It taints the dead with Abyssal energy and turns them into ghouls that wander the frozen wilderness, usually when dark mist rolls in. Its source is Rerir, one of the Five Sinners of Khaenri'ah, whose body was torn into fragments scattered across the land. It attacked Nod-Krai for years looking for the pieces of him and the power of the moons.

Most people do not know where it comes from, so folk tales fill the gap. After Rerir was expelled from Teyvat in Version 6.1, the Abyss put an imitation of Roland at its head, and when that imitation expired in 6.4 the Hunt was left leaderless and driven only by an urge to destroy.

Nature: Not a species and not a single creature. It is a distributed Abyssal phenomenon: wherever a fragment of Rerir lies, monsters gather. The ghouls themselves are described on the wiki as former humans cursed by the Abyss and doomed to wander the frozen wastes.

Archive texts describe the ghouls as spirits that could not rest, from resentment, partings or unfulfilled wishes, which the Abyss corrupted into creatures lost in the Hunt's thick mist. The Wilderness Hunter's entry adds that buried champions of a lost ancient kingdom, awakened by Abyssal taint, now treat every trespasser as prey. Their emergence is said to presage worse calamities.

Origin: Rerir was an intelligence officer of Khaenri'ah who, in despair over losing Tholindis, took Abyssal power with the other Sinners and entered a moon gate to find her; he had proposed to her but she had not yet accepted. The attempt tore his body into countless pieces scattered over Nod-Krai (All Is Foretold). The fragments became the monsters of the Wild Hunt. Nod-Krai was the first land struck by the cataclysm after Khaenri'ah, which is why the Hunt there is unusually strong.

Ghoul types: Two enemy forms are listed as the Wasteland Wild Hunt (also called Wilderness Ghouls), both elite enemies of the Abyss family with Physical attacks:
- Wilderness Hunter: the champion-like ghoul, tied in Archive text to buried warriors of a lost northern kingdom.
- Wilderness Exile: the restless-spirit ghoul, tied in Archive text to unfulfilled wishes and unresolved grief.

History: Illuga says the Lightkeepers paid in blood, three years before the events of When War Songs Rise (6.3), for the Kipumaki Cliff Hunt behaving differently from elsewhere. In the Song of the Welkin Moon Archon Quest, Flins fights it, Albedo studies it, and Rerir's role is revealed (6.1); Columbina then seals Rerir away beyond the sky while Dainsleif holds the gate open.

Distribution: Primarily Nod-Krai. The Lightkeepers also count the Abyssal phenomena at Kipumaki Cliff and elsewhere in the north as Wild Hunt, though that one behaves differently and is attributed to Rotwang and his disciples rather than Rerir. The Hunt rarely approaches Hiisi Island because the moon's power deters it.

Abilities and limits: Ghouls fight physically and hit hard in short bursts. The Hunt's wider power is its numbers, its ability to spread through the whole land from scattered fragments, and its capacity for mind-corrupting anomalies that the Lightkeepers have to clear. The Hunt can be led (Rerir, then the Roland imitation) and was able to attack Mondstadt.

Relations: Ranked as part of the Abyss. Master: Rerir, then the Roland imitation. Enemies: the Lightkeepers, the Knights of Favonius' expedition, and the Fatui, who hold the Moon Marrow Rerir wants. Dottore is the reason Rerir returned in the first place.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): ghouls are mindless and wordless; do not give them speech, plans or names. A scene works through omens: pitch-dark mist, a bell-like silence, then ghouls. Keep the larger tragedy, Rerir's love and loss, for scenes where it has been revealed.

356.content: Rerir, one of the Five Sinners of Khaenri'ah, was a normal intelligence officer who took Abyssal power after losing Tholindis, who entered a moon gate. His torn body became the Wild Hunt. After Dottore revived him he hunted for the Moon Marrow and the Three Moons' power, and he was expelled from Teyvat in Echoes of Fate. He later appears, at peace, in the moon's reflection (The First Sliver of Moonlight).

357.content: Wasteland Wild Hunt ghouls stalk the frozen wilderness when pitch-dark mist rolls in. The Hunter is bound to the champions of a lost kingdom; the Exile to restless spirits of grief. In the game they do not die at 0 HP but become Grief-Stricken and paralysed, a mechanic reflecting their sorrowful nature.

358.content: After Rerir was expelled, the Abyss produced an imitation of Roland to lead the Wild Hunt in Nod-Krai and Mondstadt. It also infested the remains of the wolf god Andrius and left his thoughts twisted. It duelled Varka, who seemed to die to reach the wolf, and expired in To Those Who Embark on the Expedition, leaving the Hunt leaderless.

359.content:
Wildlife (also: Teyvat wildlife, Teyvat fauna, wild animals of Teyvat): Teyvat's wildlife includes birds (falcons, cranes, finches, pigeons and others), beasts (boars, foxes, deer, wolves, bears, and more), fish, and small catchable animals like frogs, crabs, lizards, fireflies and crystalflies. Most flee on approach and are harmless, though boars can accidentally hurt a traveller when they charge in a panic. In game terms many drop meat, fowl or fish when killed or caught. Several species have folk reputations: kitsune, bake-danuki, wolves and owls; whales are known as gentle despite their size.

Nature: Wildlife are ordinary fauna, unlike Elemental Lifeforms and Cicins, which are made of or tied to elements. The wiki groups them into birds, beasts, fish and a miscellaneous group of small catchables (crystalflies, loaches, frogs, crabs, lizards, unagi, fireflies, scarabs and others). Nod-Krai wildlife include Frostfin Whales, which the Archive says are giant but have never actively attacked a human; they race ships and leap clear of the water as if playing. Snezhnaya has Nochhornowls (night-hunting owls), Pale-Furred Wolves and Polyarbears.

Regional variation: Examples from the Archive: Mondstadt, Nod-Krai and Snezhnaya share Pale-Furred Wolves, which the Archive says are mostly peaceful but warn intruders with long howls; Inazuma has kitsune and bake-danuki; Nod-Krai has the Frostfin Whale; Snezhnaya has the Nochhornowl and Polyarbear. Wolvendom's wolves do not flee on approach.

Scene use: Use wildlife for atmosphere: a flock lifting from a field, a boar crashing through brush, fish in a stream, or a kitsune sitting calmly near a shrine. Predators like the Polyarbear can be a real hazard on the Snezhnayan tundra. Do not give animals speech or character-level motives; canon does not.

360.comment: Wildlife: Nod-Krai wildlife and Lauma or Columbina
360.content: When Lauma or Columbina is in the player's party, some of Nod-Krai's wildlife react warmly: they dig up resources for the player or even heal and restore energy, and animals that would normally flee do not unless attacked (a gameplay behaviour). Canon gives no in-world explanation for the pattern.

361.content: The Archive describes kitsune as sly, prideful foxes said in urban legends to be very intelligent with long memories. They ignore people who come near, used to living beside humans. Legends say they were once family to the Kitsune Saiguu, and that after she disappeared the mightier Sky and Earth Kitsune turned to stone statues to await her return. As their kind dwindled they lost their mystical might and no longer speak. They are found near the Grand Narukami Shrine and just outside Inazuma City, and cannot be harmed.

362.content: Bake-danuki, also called tanuki, are a type of youkai found on Inazuma's islands (except Tsurumi Island). They look like small plump raccoons, usually with a leaf on the head and a bag around the neck. Their leader, Ioroi, is sealed inside a large statue in Chinju Forest. In play they disguise themselves as objects to prank travellers; that is a gameplay behaviour, though pranks fit their reputation.

363.content: Frostfin Whales live off Nod-Krai and are categorised as fish. The Archive calls them fierce predators to most animals, with tails that could sink a fishing boat, yet says no Frostfin Whale has ever actively attacked a human. They race ships and leap from the water, as if enjoying playing with humanity, and fisherfolk have waited hours in the cold for a glimpse. They are found south of Frostmoon Enclave, northwest of Starsand Shoal and west of South Harbor, each marked by a whale-shaped rock.

364.content: Pale-Furred Wolves live in Mondstadt, Nod-Krai and Snezhnaya. The Archive calls them solemn, noble pack hunters that rarely start attacks and instead give long warning howls. Folk tales call them rather tame, and old stories hold they descend from the Northwind, guided by a Wolf King once equal to the gods; the text says that being has long passed on. Wolves in Wolvendom do not flee when approached.

365.content: The Polyarbear is a large, thick-furred Snezhnayan animal that survives extreme cold. The Archive calls it agile despite its size, able to leap between ice floes and stalk prey silently, a top tundra hunter. It is no tame beast and some Snezhnayan regions see it as a symbol of strength. It attacks on sight and is found in Volkodlak Tundra, Everfrozen Earth and Fellfrost Peak.

366.content: Nochhornowls are Snezhnayan owls with night-sky feathers that hunt after dusk. The Archive calls them the most agile tundra hunters, skilled at disguise, observation and fast pursuit. Many hunters see them as symbols of wisdom, believe they have spirits, and say the owls sometimes guide them with messages from the forest depths. They are found across Snezhnaya.

367.content:
Youkai (also: yokai): Youkai are Inazuma's supernatural beings. They outlive humans, have their own natures, and once powerful enough can take human form. Kinds include kitsune, tengu, oni, bake-danuki (tanuki), nekomata, yumekui-baku, kappa and tsukumogami. Many died fighting the Abyss in the Cataclysm 500 years ago; today they are few and their bloodlines thin. Known present-day youkai include Yae Miko (kitsune), Yumemizuki Mizuki (baku), Kirara (nekomata), Kujou Sara (tengu) and Arataki Itto (part oni).

The most powerful are called Great Youkai; the only ones known to be alive are Yae Miko, Mizuki and the petrified bake-danuki Ioroi.

Nature: Many youkai have a true form and a human one; tails, horns or wings often show even in human shape. Inazumans believe everything has a spirit and honour local spirits at small shrines.

Not all are born youkai: Kirara was an ordinary kitten who became a two-tailed nekomata, and tsukumogami are objects that gained awareness from long exposure to strong youkai power.

History: Before Inazuma's founding, youkai roamed the islands freely (the Youkai Era). In the Archon War, Ei subdued many youkai races; those under her banner helped humans shelter in the mountains and build a city by the sea. Later the Kitsune Saiguu hosted nights of drink and stories that became the Hyakkiyakou, and the Mikawa Flower Festival also dates from this era. In the Cataclysm humans and youkai fought the Abyss together; the Kitsune Saiguu and many others died or vanished.

Society: There is no single youkai society. Some live in mountains and forests; others live openly among humans: Yae Miko is Guuji of the Grand Narukami Shrine, Kirara delivers for Komaniya Express, and Mizuki is a clinical psychologist and major shareholder of the Aisa Bathhouse.

Abilities and limits: Shape-shifting, long life, and powers by kind: kitsune and tanuki trickery, tengu flight and martial skill, oni strength, baku eating nightmares.

Relations: Relations with humans range from friendship to wariness. The gap in lifespans is a recurring sorrow; Yae Miko holds that friendships with short-lived humans are not broken but carried on in a new form.

Individuals: Besides the playable youkai: the late Kitsune Saiguu and Urakusai (kitsune), Ioroi (bake-danuki). Sayu is called a mujina but says she is fully human, and Gorou was identified as human by a bake-danuki; neither is a youkai.

Status as of 7.1: As of 7.1, youkai survive mainly in Inazuma, few and with thinning bloodlines. Ioroi remains a stone statue in Chinju Forest: during the limited-time Enchanted Tales of the Mikawa Festival event (5.4) he told Yae Miko he preferred staying petrified and that the seal's power was nearly gone anyway.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon): youkai feel old, playful and out of step with human time; many enjoy festivals, food and novels. Most present-day youkai are known to their neighbours, not hidden monsters.

368.content: "Great Youkai" is a title for exceptionally powerful youkai. Holders named in canon include the kitsune Hakushin, the Kitsune Saiguu and Urakusai (who called himself a Daiyouko), the tengu Sasayuri and Reizenbou, and the umibouzu Daikengyou. Most are dead. As of 7.1 the living Great Youkai are Yae Miko, Yumemizuki Mizuki and Ioroi. Kirara could reportedly become one if she returned to the wild, but says she never wants to.

369.content:
Yumekui-Baku (also: Yumekui Baku, baku, dream eaters, dream-eating youkai): Yumekui-baku, or baku, are lesser youkai of Inazuma who enter, shape and eat dreams. In their original form they are small, round and squishy with curly tails. Only some can take human form. Yumemizuki Mizuki is the best-known baku and works as a clinical psychologist at Aisa Bathhouse.

Baku are less famous than kitsune, oni or tengu and are traditionally seen as benevolent, carefree helpers. Today they are gradually joining human society.

Nature: Small floating dream-eaters, gentle and mostly unable to fight.

Their bodies are soft and dough-like with colourful skin, small eyes, short limbs, drooping noses and small ears, which some compare to tapirs or boars; they usually float. Those in human form tend to have large pointed ears. Prune calls them cute with dough-like bodies. The wiki notes a tapir-like belly stripe on all of them.

Abilities and limits: Enter and influence the dreams of humans and other youkai, eat them, and rarely fight.

Positive dreams taste warm and mildly sweet; nightmares taste bitter, acidic or metallic. A particularly strong nightmare acts like a toxin, causing nausea, fatigue, sharp pain, coma and possibly death. Baku can also create dreams, implant thoughts, and even enter the subconscious of a waking host whose mind is dissociated.

Society: Quiet, helpful folk with no known central leadership; rarely seen in groups.

In the youkai heyday they lived modestly, farming and weaving while offering dream-eating to those in need. At the Hyakumonogatari Taikai they served drinks or listened attentively. In the present several baku work with Mizuki at the bathhouse.

Relations: Gentle toward humans and other youkai, who rely on them for relief from nightmares.

Mizuki is a major shareholder of Aisa Bathhouse, where baku and their kin staff psychological care. Little Baku accompanies her as a companion.

Individuals: - Yumemizuki Mizuki: playable baku, clinical psychologist at Aisa Bathhouse.
- Little Baku: a baku companion of Mizuki.

History: When the Cataclysm struck, the baku hid because they were ill-suited for battle, and some still feel guilty about it. Afterwards they emerged to help with recovery, extracting the nightmares of those who had fought the Abyss and sometimes injuring themselves by overwork.

Status as of 7.1: As of 7.1 baku appear in Inazuma content from 5.4 onward, centred on Mizuki and Aisa Bathhouse; no Nod-Krai (6.x) or Snezhnaya (7.0-7.1) content adds baku lore.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon): portray baku as soft-spoken and modest, taking little for themselves. Never have a baku eat a good dream without consent.

370.content: Baku consume dreams for sustenance. Eaten dreams are forgotten by the dreamer. Mild nightmares are acid and bitter; strong ones are toxic. The unwritten baku rule forbids eating good dreams without permission.

371.content: Little Baku is a small baku companion of Mizuki, shown in its original dough-bodied form.

372.content:
Yumkasaurus (also: Yumkasaur, Yumkasaurs, Yumkasaurus Whelp, Yumkasauri): Yumkasaurs are the Dendro Saurians of Natlan: bipedal, lizard- or chameleon-like dragons with slim green bodies, feathery ears, large cheeks and a round, fluffy tail. They live in the forests of southeastern Natlan alongside the Scions of the Canopy.

They are one of six common Saurian species, each tied to a Natlan tribe. In the bestiary they are a common enemy of the Natlan Saurians group, fighting close-range with Dendro attacks.

Nature: Yumkasaurs have strong hind legs and a fluffy tail. They use their tongues as grappling hooks to swing through the air and scale walls, and keep Flamegranate pectin in their cheek pouches to spit at distant objects and wrap around them.

The Archive entry gives a legend: the original Yumkasaurs were far smaller than today's, so small they were hard to see. They roamed on the wind, clung to massive dragons, or gathered in groups that moved like clouds. After their abilities degenerated they had to take their current shape to keep their form. This is legend, not recorded history.

Society: Yumkasaurs belong to the Scions of the Canopy and live in the trees of the south-east. Like other Saurians they choose their human partners and stay in their own tribe's territory.

Signboards in the Scions' village give care advice: young Yumkasaurs like having their ears touched but dislike tail grooming, while adults enjoy tail grooming and show their tails off proudly. Saurians enter another tribe's settlement only when invited and escorted; in the game an outside Saurian is expelled by protective runes of unknown origin.

Abilities and limits: Yumkasaurs fight with their claws, tail and tongue, using Dendro power. They grapple with the tongue to swing forward and can climb cliffs, though less efficiently than Tepetlisaurs.

Gameplay (not literal lore): as enemies they whirl their tail, strike with claws after bouncing off their tail, and do a front flip using the tongue. They resist Dendro strongly. When indwelt, a Yumkasaur grapples, grabs and throws or spits objects, and takes reduced fall damage; carrying a Spore of Repose lets it make a temporary leaf to stand on.

Relations: Their human partners are the Scions of the Canopy. They are the forest counterpart of the mining Tepetlisaurs of the Children of Echoes.

Individuals: Kongamato, the ancient "Mountain King", is a Yumkasaur revered by the Scions of the Canopy. He fought beside the hero Burkina during the Cataclysm.

Characters in "A Hero's Rite" note that Yumkasaurs normally never live past a century, and suspect that Abyssal power explains his unnaturally long life. See the Saurians entry for more on him.

373.content: Yumkasaurs are Natlan's Dendro Saurians: green, slim and bushy-tailed, living in the south-eastern forests with the Scions of the Canopy. They swing on their tongues, spit Flamegranate pectin from their cheek pouches, and normally live under a century. Legend says they were once tiny and nearly invisible.

374.content:
Zombie (also: Jiangshi, the undead, Liyue zombie): In Liyue a zombie is a dead person brought back into suspended animation, by adeptal energy or by medicine. The body stays cold and stiff, and talismans help sustain the state. Two are known: Qiqi, the herb-gathering apprentice of Bubu Pharmacy, and Jialiang, a husband and father revived by Baizhu's Elixir of Immortality.

Zombies normally act on orders from whoever awakened them. Both known cases are exceptions: Qiqi gives herself orders, and Jialiang kept his own mind.

Nature: A zombie can look like an ordinary person at a glance, but the body is cold and stiff, as in rigor mortis, so zombies are usually forced to move by hopping. Talismans on the body help sustain suspended animation. Zombies need orders before they act.

Normally the awakener becomes the master and the zombie obeys; the wiki infers that an awakener could also choose to set a zombie free, since neither Qiqi nor Jialiang is controlled by anyone. Qiqi avoids hopping with daily calisthenics, done at night so Hu Tao does not see. Her appearance stays fixed at the moment of death, so estimates of her age are unreliable.

Abilities and limits: In combat Qiqi drops the self-control she normally keeps and her body returns to its undead state, giving her unusual strength and speed. Her character story notes she once sent a whole crew of Treasure Hoarders flying. Her self-given orders persist until completed or until someone cancels them by hugging her from behind and sincerely saying something like "I love you the most"; a task too hard for her can leave her stuck below a cliff, unable to give up.

Society: Zombies are not a people or community, only individual cases. Qiqi lives and works at Bubu Pharmacy under Baizhu. Hu Tao, director of the Wangsheng Funeral Parlor, wants to bury her, and Qiqi hides from her. After his revival Jialiang left Liyue with his family for Natlan, hoping the hot springs and plants there could help his condition.

Relations: Qiqi's zombie state is tied to the adepti, whose energy revived her. Jialiang's is tied instead to Baizhu's medicine, and Baizhu's elixir is described as an imitation of adeptal arts.

Individuals: Qiqi and Jialiang.

Qiqi is a playable Cryo character with a long history as a zombie. Jialiang appears only in the Heart of Healing story quest chain.

375.comment: Zombie: Qiqi's origin as a zombie
375.content: Qiqi's Character Stories relate, as a long-forgotten ancient tale, that a herb-picking girl strayed into the adepti's realm during a clash between adepti and demons, was caught in it, and received a Vision as she was dying. The adepti would not let her die and each gave her some of their strength. She woke but went berserk, unable to control the energy, and Mountain Shaper sealed her in amber. Centuries later humans found the amber and took it to the Wangsheng Funeral Parlor for burial; the road was rough and the seal was worn, so she woke, broke the amber and fled. In the hills she met Baizhu, who took her in. Because it is told as legend, details are not independently confirmed.

376.content: In the story quest The Formula for a Miracle, Jialiang, a patient with a rare heart condition who had long been sustained by god remains, agreed to let those remains be destroyed even though it meant death. Baizhu had had Qiqi prepare an Elixir of Immortality, so Jialiang woke at Bubu Pharmacy covered in talismans and was told he was now more akin to a zombie than a human. Baizhu said it was only a crude imitation of an adeptal art. Hu Tao had made the suggestion and asked Jialiang to keep it secret.

377.content: Hu Tao, the 77th-generation director of the Wangsheng Funeral Parlor, tells Qiqi it would be easier if she just let herself be buried. Qiqi has no wish to be buried, exercises when no one is about, and has learned hiding places to avoid her. Qiqi calls her face punchable and holds a grudge against her,.
